title: Refactoring in safe steps
idea: Refactoring is changing the structure of code without changing what it does, in small steps that tests confirm one at a time.
points: First pin today's behaviour with characterization tests, odd inputs included.
Make one small named move, run the tests, then commit.
Each code smell points to a known move, like Extract Function.
Never mix a refactor and a new feature in the same commit.

hero.caption: Name the smell first; the move follows from it.

code.title: Before
code.caption: Run it and keep the output. That output is the behaviour the refactor must preserve.

code.title: After
code.caption: Same output, three named pieces. A new type is now one entry in `rules`.

walk.text: Replace Magic Literal: `BOOK_DISCOUNT = 0.1` names the 10% hidden in the unexplained `0.9`.
Replace Conditional with a lookup: the `if/else` chain becomes a map from type to rule.
`keep` preserves the old fall-through for unknown types like `misc`.
Extract Function: `subtotal` names the price-times-quantity step.
`invoiceLine` now reads as a sentence: pick a rule, apply it, format.

pitfalls: Do not refactor code with no tests; write characterization tests for today's output first.
Check the default branch: dropping an implicit `else` silently changes behaviour.
Keep each step small enough to undo; a big-bang rewrite is not refactoring.

quiz.q: A refactor dropped the fallback. What does this print?
quiz.why: `rules['pen']` is `undefined`, and calling `undefined` throws a `TypeError`. The old `if/else` left unknown types unchanged.

takeaway: Tests first, one small move, tests again, commit.

starters: How do I write characterization tests for messy legacy code?
When should I replace a conditional with polymorphism instead of a lookup table?
How do I refactor safely when there are no tests at all?
